rows.stem: The \(13^{\text{th}}\) term from the end of the A.P. : \(20, 13, 6, -1, \ldots\ldots, -148\) is :
rows.solution:
Read from the end, the A.P. is \(-148, -141, -134, \ldots\) with first term \(-148\) and common difference \(7\) (the original difference is \(13 - 20 = -7\)).

The 13th term from the end is \(-148 + 12 \times 7 = -148 + 84 = -64\), which is option (D) \(-64\).

rows.subtopic: Probability with Cards, Dice and Coins
rows.stem: Two dice are rolled together. What is the probability of getting a sum greater than 10 ?
rows.solution:
Two dice give \(6 \times 6 = 36\) equally likely outcomes. A sum greater than 10 means a sum of 11 or 12: \((5, 6)\), \((6, 5)\) and \((6, 6)\), 3 outcomes.

\(P = \dfrac{3}{36} = \dfrac{1}{12}\), which is option (C) \(\dfrac{1}{12}\).

rows.stem: If end points of a diameter of a circle are \((-5, 4)\) and \((1, 0)\), then the radius of the circle is :
rows.solution:
The diameter is the distance between \((-5, 4)\) and \((1, 0)\): \(\sqrt{(1 + 5)^2 + (0 - 4)^2} = \sqrt{36 + 16} = \sqrt{52} = 2\sqrt{13}\) units.

The radius is half of this, \(\sqrt{13}\) units, which is option (B) \(\sqrt{13}\) units.

rows.subtopic: Forming a Quadratic Polynomial from its Zeroes
rows.stem: The number of polynomials having zeroes \(-1\) and 2 is :
rows.solution:
A polynomial with zeroes \(-1\) and 2 has the form \(k(x + 1)(x - 2)\) for any non-zero constant k. Each value of k gives a different polynomial with the same zeroes, so there are infinitely many.

This is option (D) infinite.

rows.stem: The common difference of the A.P. whose \(n^{\text{th}}\) term is given by \(a_n = 5n - 7\) is :

rows.subtopic: Section Formula and Ratio of Division
rows.stem: Find the ratio in which line \(y = x\) divides the line segment joining the points \((6, -3)\) and \((1, 6)\).
rows.solution:
Let the line \(y = x\) meet the segment joining \((6, -3)\) and \((1, 6)\) at \(P(x, y)\), dividing it in the ratio \(k : 1\) (measured from \((6, -3)\)).

By the section formula, \(x = \dfrac{k \times 1 + 1 \times 6}{k + 1} = \dfrac{k + 6}{k + 1}\) and \(y = \dfrac{k \times 6 + 1 \times (-3)}{k + 1} = \dfrac{6k - 3}{k + 1}\).

P lies on \(y = x\), so \(k + 6 = 6k - 3\), giving \(5k = 9\) and \(k = \dfrac{9}{5}\).

The ratio is \(9 : 5\). (Check: the point is \(\left(\dfrac{39}{14}, \dfrac{39}{14}\right)\), which does lie on \(y = x\).)

rows.stem: In the given figure, PQ is a chord of the circle centered at O. PT is a tangent to the circle at P. If \(\angle QPT = 55^\circ\), then find \(\angle PRQ\).
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - only the drawing places R on the minor arc PQ (on the same side of PQ as T), which makes angle PRQ an angle in the minor segment (125 degrees) rather than one in the major segment (55 degrees); it also shows the dashed radii OP and OQ. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
In the figure, R lies on the minor arc PQ, on the same side of the chord PQ as T. So \(\angle PRQ\) is an angle in the minor segment, and it stands on the major arc PQ.

The radius OP is perpendicular to the tangent PT, so \(\angle OPT = 90^\circ\) and \(\angle OPQ = 90^\circ - 55^\circ = 35^\circ\).

\(OP = OQ\) (radii), so \(\angle OQP = 35^\circ\) and \(\angle POQ = 180^\circ - 35^\circ - 35^\circ = 110^\circ\).

The major arc PQ subtends the reflex angle \(POQ = 360^\circ - 110^\circ = 250^\circ\) at the centre, and the angle it subtends at R on the remaining part of the circle is half of this:

\(\angle PRQ = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 250^\circ = 125^\circ\).

(Another route gives the same answer: by the alternate segment theorem, a point on the major arc sees PQ at \(55^\circ\). Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to \(180^\circ\), so R on the minor arc sees it at \(180^\circ - 55^\circ = 125^\circ\). The answer \(55^\circ\) would be right only if R were on the major arc.)

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.stem: A 2-digit number is seven times the sum of its digits. The number formed by reversing the digits is 18 less than the given number. Find the given number.
rows.solution:
Let the units digit be x and the tens digit be y, so the number is \(10y + x\).

The number is seven times the sum of its digits: \(10y + x = 7(x + y)\), so \(3y - 6x = 0\), that is \(y = 2x\) ... (i)

Reversing the digits gives \(10x + y\), which is 18 less: \((10y + x) - (10x + y) = 18\), so \(9y - 9x = 18\), that is \(y - x = 2\) ... (ii)

Substituting (i) in (ii): \(2x - x = 2\), so \(x = 2\) and \(y = 4\).

The number is 42. (Check: \(7 \times (4 + 2) = 42\) and \(42 - 24 = 18\).)

rows.subtopic: Sum of First n Terms of an AP
rows.stem: In an A.P., the sum of the first n terms is given by \(S_n = 6n - n^2\). Find its \(30^{\text{th}}\) term.

The angle of elevation of the top of a vertical tower from a point P on the ground is \(60^\circ\). From another point Q, 10 m vertically above the first point P, its angle of elevation is \(30^\circ\). Find :

(a) The height of the tower.

(b) The distance of the point P from the foot of the tower.

(c) The distance of the point P from the top of the tower.
rows.solution:
Let AD be the tower of height h m, with A its foot and D its top, and let \(AP = x\) m. Q is 10 m vertically above P, so the horizontal line through Q meets AD at a point 10 m above A, and the part of the tower above that point is \((h - 10)\) m.

From P: \(\tan 60^\circ = \dfrac{h}{x} = \sqrt{3}\), so \(h = \sqrt{3}\,x\) ... (i)

From Q: \(\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{h - 10}{x} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), so \(h = 10 + \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{3}}\) ... (ii)

From (i) and (ii): \(\sqrt{3}\,x = 10 + \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{3}}\). Multiplying by \(\sqrt{3}\): \(3x = 10\sqrt{3} + x\), so \(2x = 10\sqrt{3}\) and \(x = 5\sqrt{3}\).

(a) The height of the tower is \(h = \sqrt{3} \times 5\sqrt{3} = 15\) m.

(b) The distance of P from the foot of the tower is \(x = 5\sqrt{3}\) m (about \(8{\cdot}66\) m).

(c) In right triangle DAP, \(\cos 60^\circ = \dfrac{AP}{PD}\), so \(PD = \dfrac{5\sqrt{3}}{1/2} = 10\sqrt{3}\) m (about \(17{\cdot}32\) m). (Check: \(PD^2 = 75 + 225 = 300\).)
